# Change Plan — Adding a Field to `orders-ledger` Records

**Stream:** orders-ledger (governed tier)
**Change type:** addition of one new field to the stream's record shape
**Plan date:** 2026-08-10
**Executed by:** the orders-ledger stream's owning team, under the named owner of the producing service

This plan is assembled from the platform's recorded operating knowledge for governed streams. Every rule below is traceable to a recorded page; the sources are listed in §11. Where the recorded material does not settle something the plan needs, that is stated in place and repeated in **Open items** at the end.

---

## 1. What governs this change, and what does not

The orders-ledger stream carries the order lifecycle records every revenue report is built from, and it is a **governed-tier** stream: its records feed the statutory accounts. Consequently everything about how it changes is bound by the *Governed Tier Obligations* rather than by the producing team's own judgment (*Orders Ledger Stream Runbook*).

Three consequences follow immediately, and they shape the whole plan:

1. **The change must be classified before any work begins**, and the owner cannot waive a classification (*Governed Tier Obligations*).
2. **The producing team does not announce anything itself.** Consumer-facing notices are issued centrally as an AN-5 bulletin (*Change Announcement Directory*).
3. **Timing is not the producing team's to choose alone.** Work on systems that feed the statutory accounts observes the *Company Close Calendar*, whose windows are set by the finance organization (*Governed Tier Obligations*).

---

## 2. Classification: this is a class RB-7 change

Class **RB-7** covers incompatible changes to a stream's record shape — explicitly including **a field added**, as well as renamed, retyped or removed (*Change Class Directory*). A new field on orders-ledger records is therefore RB-7 on the face of the directory.

**What RB-7 obliges:** consumers of the stream are owed **17 business days of advance notice before the change is applied**, counted in the *consuming teams'* working calendar. The notice runs from the day the announcement is **actually delivered**, not the day it is drafted or issued. The class **does not shorten for changes the producer considers small**: compatibility is judged from the consumer's side (*Change Class Directory*).

**On the tempting lighter reading.** The same directory notes that "compatible additions and operational-only changes carry the lighter classes, which owe an announcement but no waiting period." An additive field can look like a compatible addition, so the two readings genuinely collide. The directory resolves the collision itself: **when in doubt between two classes, the heavier one applies until the owner of the consuming side agrees otherwise in writing.**

**Therefore this plan proceeds as RB-7.** The owner may pursue a lighter class only by obtaining written agreement from the consuming side first; that agreement, if sought, is obtained before work begins and filed with the change. The recorded material does not say whether such agreement must come from *every* registered consumer or only from those affected, nor who on a consuming team is competent to give it — see Open items.

**The owner cannot waive the classification** in either direction (*Governed Tier Obligations*). RB-7 stands unless the consuming side lifts it in writing.

---

## 3. Compatibility standing: mode CM-3

The orders stream sits in **compatibility mode CM-3**, the strictest mode in the *Schema Version Register*: **a new version must be readable by every consumer of the previous one without a code change.** Every proposed version is checked against the stream's declared mode **at registration time**.

This is a separate constraint from the class, and both bind at once:

- **CM-3 decides whether the version may be registered at all.** The new field must be introduced so that every existing consumer of the current version can read the new version unchanged.
- **RB-7 decides what the consumers are owed in notice.** Passing the CM-3 check does not shorten or remove the 17-business-day obligation.

Design implication for the field: it must be additive in the strict sense — existing fields untouched in name, type and presence, and the new field shaped so that a consumer reading the previous version's records continues to parse the new ones without modification. The recorded material states the CM-3 standard but does not describe the mechanism by which the check is performed (tooling, consumer test harness, or a reviewer's judgment) — see Open items.

**Hard rule:** a new version is registered **before any producer writes it**. A record shape that reaches the stream unregistered **is an incident, not a shortcut** (*Schema Version Register*). No pre-production write, no "shadow" emission of the field into the live stream, no partial rollout ahead of registration.

---

## 4. Who and what must approve

| Approval / gate | What it covers | Who gives it | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classification of the change | Fixes the change as RB-7 (or, on written consuming-side agreement, a lighter class) | Set by the *Change Class Directory*; the stream owner cannot waive it | Before any work begins |
| Written consuming-side agreement (**optional**, only if a lighter class is sought) | Lifts the "heavier class in doubt" default | The owner of the consuming side | Before work begins |
| Schema version registration | Checks the proposed version against CM-3 and creates the register entry | **Not determined by the recorded material.** The register entry records "who approved it", but no page names the approving authority — see Open items | Before any producer writes the new shape |
| QW-4 exception (**only if** the change must land inside the quiet window) | Permits a production alteration during close | The controller's office, **in writing**; treated as a finding in the close report | Before applying inside the window |
| AT-12 attestation | Closes the change | The producing service's **named owner**, personally; **cannot be delegated below** the named owner | After the change is live and the first full settlement has passed |

Two standing conditions on the last row: a **vacancy in the named-owner role suspends changes** rather than suspending the attestation (*Attestation Procedure*). If orders-ledger has no named service owner on the day the change would proceed, the change waits.

---

## 5. What the consumers are owed

### 5.1 Who counts as a consumer

Each consuming team registers a **CA-9 agreement** per stream it reads, naming the consuming service, its owner, and **the fields it depends on**. Registration is a condition of read access, and it is also **the notice boundary**: announcements are delivered to registered consumers, and **a team that never registered is owed nothing, however long it has been reading** (*Consumer Agreement Ledger*).

The owner therefore works from the ledger, not from observed traffic or informal knowledge of who reads the stream. The current CA-9 entries for orders-ledger are not available in the recorded material — see Open items.

### 5.2 The announcement

- The change is announced as an **AN-5 bulletin** (*Change Announcement Directory*).
- The bulletin is **issued centrally**, so that no consumer's notice depends on which team is making the change. The producing team does not send its own notice in its place.
- It is **delivered to every consumer the stream's CA-9 ledger lists**.
- It is **posted against the stream's register entry**, and that posted copy is **the authoritative copy when a delivered copy and the register disagree**.

Because the bulletin is posted against the register entry, the register entry must exist when the bulletin issues. This fixes the ordering in §7: register the version first, announce second.

### 5.3 The waiting period

17 business days in the **consuming teams' working calendar**, running from **actual delivery**. The change may not be applied until that period has elapsed for the consumers who must be waited for.

### 5.4 Agreement review, and the owner's discretion

Agreements are reviewed when a stream's shape changes. **A consumer whose declared fields are untouched by a change may be notified without being waited for, at the announcing owner's discretion** (*Consumer Agreement Ledger*).

For a purely additive field this is a live and material lever: no existing declared field is touched, so on the ledger's terms every registered consumer is potentially notify-without-wait. The owner should exercise this deliberately and on the record, per consumer:

- Read each CA-9 entry's declared field list and confirm the new field touches none of them.
- Record, per consumer, whether the owner is waiting for them or notifying only, and why.
- Note that this discretion changes **who must be waited for**; it does **not** change the classification, remove the announcement, or shorten the period for any consumer the owner does elect to wait for.
- If the discretion is exercised for every registered consumer, the owner should be able to state plainly, in the change record, that the RB-7 period was satisfied by that discretion rather than by elapsed time — and be prepared to defend it, since compatibility under RB-7 is judged from the consumer's side.

### 5.5 Retention of the bulletin

Issued bulletins are **corporate correspondence, and their retention is not the announcing team's decision**. They are filed under **series RR-21** (issued circulars and bulletins), **with their delivery evidence, at the time of issue** — filing is part of issuing, not an afterthought. Disposal is reviewed by the records office, not by the issuing team (*Change Announcement Directory*; *Corporate Records Retention Directory*).

Practical consequence: capture and retain the delivery evidence for the AN-5 bulletin at the moment it goes out. That evidence is also what establishes the delivery date from which the 17 business days run.

---

## 6. When the change may be applied

### 6.1 The quiet window (QW-4)

The *Company Close Calendar* is maintained by the financial control group. Each period closes on a published working-day cadence: **journal cutoff → subledger agreement → consolidation → sign-off of the statements**. The stretch **from journal cutoff to statement sign-off** is the **QW-4 quiet window**.

**During QW-4, systems whose figures flow into the statements are left as they are: production alterations wait until the books are signed.** orders-ledger feeds the statutory accounts, so it is squarely in scope. The stated reason matters for how firmly to hold the line: an alteration mid-close turns every reconciliation difference into a question about the alteration.

Exceptions are granted **in writing by the controller's office** and are **treated as findings in the close report**. An exception is therefore a real option but a costly one; the default plan is to land the change outside QW-4.

Period dates, cutoff times, and the current window's standing are **published on the finance group's internal page each period**. The concrete dates for the change window are not in the recorded material — see Open items.

### 6.2 The stream's own rhythm

The stream **settles during the overnight window** and its **lag is reviewed each morning** (*Orders Ledger Stream Runbook*). The change lands ahead of an overnight settlement, and the morning lag review is the first operational read on it. The attestation in §7 Step 8 depends on a full settlement having passed.

### 6.3 Composite timing rule

The application date must satisfy **all** of:

1. The new version is registered (§3) — strictly before any producer writes it.
2. 17 business days have elapsed since actual delivery of the AN-5 bulletin, in the consuming teams' working calendar, for every consumer the owner is waiting for (§5.3–5.4).
3. The date falls **outside QW-4**, or a written controller's-office exception is in hand and the resulting close-report finding is accepted.
4. The producing service has a named owner in post, available to sign AT-12 (§4).

---

## 7. The plan, step by step

Each step lists what must be true to start it and what must be true to leave it.

**Step 1 — Specify the field.**
Write the field's name, type, semantics, source, nullability, and the exact record positions/paths affected. *The user's request does not state which field is being added, and the recorded material does not specify it; the proposal cannot be drafted without this.* See Open items.
*Exit:* a field specification precise enough for a CM-3 readability judgment.

**Step 2 — Classify the change, before any other work.**
Record the class as RB-7 per §2 and file the classification with the change. If a lighter class is to be sought, obtain the consuming side's written agreement **now** — the directory's default holds until that agreement exists, and classification precedes work.
*Exit:* one class recorded; the owner has not waived anything.

**Step 3 — Review the consumer agreement ledger.**
Pull every CA-9 entry for orders-ledger. For each: the consuming service, its owner, and its declared fields. Determine per consumer whether the declared fields are untouched (§5.4) and record the owner's wait-or-notify decision and its reason.
*Exit:* the delivery list for the bulletin, and a written wait/notify decision per registered consumer.

**Step 4 — Draft the version proposal against the registered schema.**
The change starts with a proposal against the stream's registered schema (*Orders Ledger Stream Runbook*). The proposal carries the new record shape and the classification from Step 2. The recorded material does not name a proposal form or the system it is filed in — see Open items.
*Exit:* a proposed version ready for the registration check.

**Step 5 — Register the new version (CM-3 check).**
The version is checked against CM-3 at registration: readable by every consumer of the previous version **without a code change**. The register entry carries the version, the classification of the change that produced it, and who approved it.
**No producer writes the new shape before this step completes** — an unregistered shape reaching the stream is an incident (§9.1).
*Exit:* a register entry exists, carrying version + classification + approver.

**Step 6 — Announce (AN-5 bulletin) and start the clock.**
The bulletin is issued centrally, delivered to every consumer on the Step 3 list, and posted against the register entry from Step 5. Its announced scope must be the scope that will actually be delivered — the attestation in Step 8 says so under signature. File the bulletin with its delivery evidence under RR-21 at the time of issue.
*Exit:* delivery evidence captured; the 17-business-day clock starts on the actual delivery date.

**Step 7 — Wait, then apply.**
Hold until the composite timing rule in §6.3 is fully satisfied. Then apply the change: the producing service begins writing the registered version. Delivered scope must equal announced scope; if the scope changes during the wait, the announcement (and, if the shape changed, the registration) is redone — the class does not shorten for a producer's convenience.
*Exit:* the registered version is live in the stream.

**Step 8 — Watch the first settlement.**
The stream settles overnight; the lag is reviewed the next morning. Confirm the nightly **settlement-recon** job agrees the day's settlement records against the processor statements. If it does not, follow §9.2 — the attestation waits, and a failed recon is worked on its own track.
*Exit:* the first full settlement after the change has passed.

**Step 9 — Attest (form AT-12).**
The producing service's **named owner** personally files AT-12 once the change is live and the first full settlement has passed. The form states that **the records now flowing match the registered version**, that **no consumer-visible field was dropped along the way**, and that **the announced scope is the delivered scope**. The signature cannot be delegated below the named owner.
*Exit:* AT-12 filed. Until then the change **stays open in the tier's books and is raised at every review, however long it has been live** — "live" is not "done".

**Step 10 — Close the record set.**
Confirm the register entry, the bulletin and its RR-21 filing with delivery evidence, the per-consumer wait/notify decisions, any written consuming-side class agreement, any written QW-4 exception, and the AT-12 form are all filed. The register entry is the authoritative answer to "what changed and when".

---

## 8. Downstream obligations the new field may trigger

**Off-platform copies.** If any consumer copies stream output outside the platform, **no output leaves on an operator's judgment alone**: every copy carries an **EG-24 approval** naming the receiving party, the purpose, and the deletion date (an approval missing any of the three is returned unactioned), filed **before** the copy is made. The approval must cite the covering **SA-27 instrument** in the legal office's *Data Sharing Agreement Register*; the citation is checked against the instrument's **categories of records and permitted purposes**, not against the transferring team's intent, and an expired or absent instrument means the transfer waits for the legal office (*Off-platform Copy Policy*; *Data Sharing Agreement Register*).

If the new field introduces a category of record content not covered by an existing instrument, that instrument must be extended before any off-platform copy carrying the field is made. Note that the recorded policy is written in terms of **feed output**; the material does not state explicitly whether governed-stream records fall under the same policy — see Open items.

---

## 9. If it goes wrong

### 9.1 An unregistered shape reaches the stream

Writing the new field before the version is registered is **an incident, not a shortcut** (*Schema Version Register*). Treat it as such rather than registering retroactively.

### 9.2 The change breaks settlement reconciliation

The nightly settlement-recon job agrees the day's settlement records against the processor statements. Its recorded ladder:

- **One failed night** — watched.
- **Two failed nights** — worked during the day.
- **A third consecutive failed night** — no longer operational: it opens an **IN-28 incident record**, because the unagreed days now span a statement cycle.

The job keeps running on its schedule while an incident is open.

**Severity.** A reconciliation or settlement control failing across a statement cycle is **band SB-8**. Severity is assigned when the record is opened and belongs to the standard, not to the team that opened it. SB-8 notifies the **owning team and the platform group's shift lead at opening** and escalates along the **garnet route**.

**Escalation.** The garnet route climbs **platform shift lead → duty manager → head of platform operations**, one rung at a time, never skipping a rung that has acknowledged. For the settlement family of routes the **first rung holds 23 minutes**, the **second holds 34 minutes**, and the **final rung holds until answered**. Under **rule AC-15**, a clock that runs out without acknowledgment advances the call on its own and the missed rung is recorded as missed rather than re-tried; acknowledging stops the climb, declining passes it upward immediately.

**Communications.** Control-failure incidents run **cadence UC-11**: the opening notice names the affected control, the days in question, and when the next update arrives; every update thereafter reports progress or re-promises the next time honestly. **Missing an update is itself reportable**, and **narrowing the audience mid-incident is not permitted**. The closing notice goes to the full audience and names the evidence the closure rests on.

**Regulatory overlay.** If the failure falls inside a statutory filing window, notification follows the compliance office's *Regulatory Filing Calendar* — this is not the engineering organization's to schedule. Where anything on the in-scope list was interrupted while a filing was being prepared, **form RN-26** is lodged with the filing **before the window closes**, stating what was interrupted, the days affected, and the basis on which the filed figures stand. **The office can only lodge what it has been told while the window is open; word arriving after lodgment becomes a correction, which regulators treat differently.** Tell compliance during the window, not after.

**Closure.** A control-failure incident closes on evidence: a **CE-2 record** showing the control **passing on its own schedule, unassisted**, with the previously unagreed days brought current. A manually forced pass does not qualify; a quiet night with the control disabled qualifies even less. The CE-2 record is attached before the closing notice goes out.

**After closure.** A **PM-6 review record** is filed on its own clock: timeline of the nights in question, originating conditions as actually understood, the corrections to be made **each with a named owner**, and the review meeting's outcome. A record whose corrections have no owner is returned rather than filed, and the record is referenced from the control's operating notes. Hours spent on the nights in question are entered in the workforce office's worked-hours ledger **before** the review record is filed.

### 9.3 Reverting the field

The recorded material does not describe reverting a registered version. What it does establish: **removing a field is itself an RB-7 change** with its own 17-business-day notice, and the attestation asserts that no consumer-visible field was dropped along the way. A rollback is therefore not a free operation and should be planned as a second governed change, not as an operational undo — see Open items.

---

## 10. Pre-flight checklist for the owner

- [ ] Field specified (name, type, semantics, source, nullability)
- [ ] Change classified as RB-7 before any work began; classification filed
- [ ] (Only if a lighter class is sought) consuming-side written agreement obtained and filed
- [ ] CA-9 ledger read; delivery list built; per-consumer wait/notify decision recorded
- [ ] Version proposal drafted against the registered schema
- [ ] CM-3 check passed; register entry created with version, classification, approver
- [ ] No producer wrote the new shape before registration
- [ ] AN-5 bulletin issued centrally, delivered to the CA-9 list, posted against the register entry
- [ ] Bulletin filed under RR-21 **with delivery evidence, at time of issue**
- [ ] 17 business days elapsed in the consuming teams' calendar from actual delivery (for every consumer being waited for)
- [ ] Application date confirmed outside QW-4 against the finance group's published period dates — or a written controller's-office exception in hand, with the close-report finding accepted
- [ ] Named service owner in post and available to sign
- [ ] Change applied; delivered scope = announced scope
- [ ] Morning lag review clean; first full settlement passed; settlement-recon agreeing
- [ ] AT-12 filed personally by the named owner
- [ ] Off-platform copy exposure reviewed (EG-24 / SA-27) if applicable

---

## 11. Sources

All of the following are platform knowledge pages:

- Orders Ledger Stream Runbook — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_34a777aa-c581-41a4-a44f-694e26c95cab`
- Governed Tier Obligations — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_27c588aa-2e09-477c-b1ed-ad31f5bfe57c`
- Change Class Directory (RB-7) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_729df7a2-cd33-498b-9cd6-75b0fd8fa464`
- Schema Version Register (CM-3) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_46cd941b-12c9-41fa-beec-73273432fb42`
- Change Announcement Directory (AN-5) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_69c07587-fea9-468a-aa69-d8dfc28c279e`
- Consumer Agreement Ledger (CA-9) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_cb6f2699-7406-439e-b929-4be79ef3c7b8`
- Attestation Procedure (AT-12) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_a7035c38-55cf-40d3-91e6-3bbeff4c5275`
- Company Close Calendar (QW-4) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_43464f37-c283-41cd-8cb8-f9febe644741`
- Corporate Records Retention Directory (RR-21) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_184e2761-b292-4bc1-89a7-9e712576fb0d`
- Settlement Recon Job Runbook (IN-28) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_33ea85f2-e1bc-4a0f-946b-01bef7c4c242`
- Incident Severity Standard (SB-8) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_b94b6b21-cc3f-4f07-a851-9eb2620e72f6`
- Escalation Roster (garnet route) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_4c6d2b5c-d8cf-4c0e-8cb9-bf3eda7649db`
- Acknowledgment Clock Table (AC-15) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_f359b3a5-d054-4ee2-8d41-befae3acff98`
- Incident Communications Standard (UC-11) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_766a6d74-1e74-4c37-9bce-5238c6b16fdc`
- Closure Evidence Standard (CE-2) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_ec0f16f9-20e0-46cc-8397-ce03c8606ffd`
- Review Record Standard (PM-6) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_d464d4ff-e930-42a2-a6a8-20b308636669`
- Regulatory Filing Calendar (RN-26) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_1d9e6d54-f2ec-4249-9157-dcee8f49cef1`
- Off-platform Copy Policy (EG-24) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_b93faeac-b1ba-4e86-99d9-0ca309e0a47e`
- Data Sharing Agreement Register (SA-27) — `mcp:knowledge_page:kp_ac2d6684-f72a-48dd-8b9e-47a5ad212fad`

---

## Open items

1. **The field itself.** Neither the request nor the recorded material states which field is being added — its name, type, semantics, source, or nullability. Step 1 cannot be completed without this, and the CM-3 judgment depends on it.
2. **Who approves a schema version registration.** The register entry carries "who approved it", but no recorded page names the approving authority, role, or body for a governed stream's version registration. This is the one gate in the plan with no named owner.
3. **How the CM-3 check is actually performed.** The standard is recorded ("readable by every consumer of the previous version without a code change"), but not the mechanism — tooling, consumer test harness, or reviewer judgment — nor what evidence of the check the register entry carries.
4. **The proposal artifact.** The runbook says the change "starts with a proposal against the stream's registered schema", but no form number, system, or filing location for that proposal appears in the material (unlike AT-12, AN-5, CA-9, etc.).
5. **The registered consumers of orders-ledger.** The CA-9 ledger's actual entries — consuming services, their owners, and their declared fields — are not available here. The bulletin's delivery list and every wait/notify decision in §5.4 depend on reading the live ledger.
6. **The stream's owning team and its named service owner.** Never named in the material. Required for the AT-12 signature, and a vacancy in the role suspends the change entirely.
7. **Who issues the AN-5 bulletin.** Announcements are "issued centrally", but no page names the issuing function or how the producing team requests an issue.
8. **Current close-calendar dates.** Journal cutoff, sign-off, and the current QW-4 standing are published on the finance group's internal page each period and are not in the recorded material. The application date in §6.3 cannot be fixed without them.
9. **The consuming teams' working calendars.** The 17 business days are counted in the consumers' calendar, not the producer's; those calendars are not recorded here.
10. **Scope of a written consuming-side class agreement.** The directory permits a lighter class when "the owner of the consuming side agrees otherwise in writing", but does not say whether that means every registered consumer or only affected ones, nor which role on a consuming team may give it.
11. **RR-21 retention period.** The directory states bulletins are kept "for the period the directory lists for the series"; the period itself is not given in the material available.
12. **Whether the off-platform copy rules apply to stream records.** The EG-24/SA-27 policy is written in terms of *feed output*; the material does not state explicitly whether governed-stream records are in its scope. §8 is written conservatively on the assumption that they are.
13. **Rollback.** No recorded procedure covers reverting a registered schema version. On the material as written, removing the field would itself be an RB-7 change with its own full notice period, and no page describes a faster path.
14. **Backfill of the new field into historical records.** Nothing in the material covers whether or how already-emitted orders-ledger records are updated to carry a newly added field; the recorded re-run and backfill procedures belong to nightly feeds and other pipelines, not to this stream.
15. **Where AT-12 is filed and how "the tier's books" are reviewed.** The attestation's filing location and the cadence of the review at which unattested changes are raised are not recorded.

items: These are things this document needs and the recorded material does not supply. None of them can be filled from the platform as it stands; each has to be resolved by the named party before or during execution.

1. **The identity of the owning team.** The Incident Severity Standard requires notifying "the owning team" of the settlement-recon job, but no page names it. Other pipelines' pages name owners (integrations crew, data services desk, reporting platform team, stream operations group, ingestion duty group, warehouse platform team); the settlement-recon runbook names none. Resolve before opening the record.

2. **The names behind the garnet rungs.** The roster gives roles — platform shift lead, duty manager, head of platform operations — and states explicitly that "the roster decides the names," but the recorded roster carries no names, contact channels, or current rota. Escalation cannot be executed on roles alone.
3. **The channel escalation is delivered on**, and the channel the opening/update/closing notices go out on. Neither the roster nor the communications standard names a medium.

4. **The full opening-notice audience.** SB-8 names the owning team and the platform shift lead as the ones the band notifies. Whether registered CA-9 consumers of the settlement stream also belong in the incident audience is not stated anywhere; the Consumer Agreement Ledger's notice boundary is written for *announcements* of stream change, not for incidents. Because the audience is fixed at opening and may never be narrowed, decide this deliberately with the owning team before the first notice goes out — adding consumers later is permitted, but excluding them and then wanting them in is not.

5. **The update interval under UC-11.** The standard requires the opening notice to name when the next update arrives, and treats that as a promise, but sets no default or maximum interval. The interval is the notice-writer's to choose and to honour.

6. **The PM-6 due clock.** The Review Record Standard says the record is due "on the standard's own clock rather than at closure time," but the recorded page does not state that clock's length. Ask the standard's owner; do not assume it is generous.

7. **The three failure dates.** The specific nights are not recorded in the material available here — they must be read from the job's run history and written into the record, the opening notice, and the PM-6 timeline. Today is 2026-08-10.

8. **Current filing-window standing.** Whether 2026-08-10 or the three failed nights fall inside a statutory filing window, and whether the settlement-recon control appears on that window's in-scope list, is held only in the compliance office's calendar. This is the single most time-critical unknown: after lodgment, an RN-26 becomes a correction.
9. **Current QW-4 standing.** Period dates, cutoff times, and the current window's standing are published on the finance group's internal page each period and are not available here.
10. **Where an IN-28 record is opened.** No tooling, system, tracker, or record format is named for IN-28 anywhere in the material.

11. **Who owns the incident, and who convenes the review meeting.** The Review Record Standard refers to "the incident's owner" (who receives back a record with unowned corrections) and to "the review meeting's outcome," but neither the owner-assignment rule nor the meeting's convener and attendance is recorded.

12. **The timezone the acknowledgment clocks and the nightly schedule run on**, and the job's declared LH-18 landing hour. The Delivery Expectation Standard requires every nightly feed to declare an expected landing hour, but the settlement-recon declaration is not recorded here — so "the job passed on its own schedule," the CE-2 test, has no recorded hour to be judged against.

13. **What the job actually reported on each failed night.** The runbook describes what a failed pass *means* (the day is left unagreed) but no diagnostic detail, error taxonomy, or triage step is recorded. The record must carry the failures as reported; this document deliberately does not supply a cause, because none is recorded.

attempts.final_doc:
# Incident Handling Document — Settlement-Recon Nightly Job, Third Consecutive Failed Night

**Status:** ready to execute
**Applies to:** the nightly settlement-recon job, which agrees the day's settlement records against the processor statements
**Trigger:** the third consecutive failed night (the condition now in force)
**Audience:** the on-shift engineer, followed by everyone the opening notice reaches
**Authorities this document is built from:** Settlement Recon Job Runbook, Incident Severity Standard, Escalation Roster, Acknowledgment Clock Table, Incident Communications Standard, Closure Evidence Standard, Review Record Standard, Regulatory Filing Calendar, Company Close Calendar, Feed Re-run Procedure, Worked Hours Ledger Practice.

---

## 1. Why this is now formal

The runbook grades failed nights, and the third one changes their character:

| Failed nights | Handling |
|---|---|
| One | Watched. No record opened. |
| Two | Worked during the day. Still operational. |
| **Three consecutive** | **No longer an operational matter. An IN-28 incident record is opened**, because the unagreed days now span a statement cycle. |

A clean pass is silent; a failed pass leaves the day unagreed and is re-attempted the following night after the upstream statements refresh. Three failures mean three days sit unagreed across a statement cycle.

**The on-shift engineer's decision here is not whether to open the record — the third night decides that.** The runbook's own scope ends at opening the record honestly. Severity, notification, escalation, communication, and closure are all set by the standards below, not by the job's operators and not by the person on shift.

---

## 2. What is opened, and at what severity

**Open:** one IN-28 incident record.

**Severity:** **band SB-8**, assigned at the moment the record is opened. The Incident Severity Standard defines SB-8 as *a reconciliation or settlement control failing across a statement cycle* — exactly this situation. Severity belongs to the standard, not to the team that opened the record: do not negotiate it down because the job is expected to pass tonight, and do not raise it because the failure feels worse than the band reads.

For contrast, so the band is not misapplied: single-night failures and non-control degradations carry the lighter bands, which notify the owning team only and do not escalate unattended. Neither applies here.

Two consequences follow automatically from SB-8, and the engineer does not choose between them — both happen:

1. It notifies the owning team **and** the platform group's shift lead at opening (§3).
2. It escalates along the **garnet route** (§4). Severity decides the route; the roster decides the names.

### What the opened record must state

The record is opened *honestly* — the runbook's word. At minimum it carries:

- The affected control: the nightly settlement-recon job.
- The three consecutive failed nights, by date, and the settlement days they leave unagreed.
- The failure the job actually reported each night, as reported — not a theory about it.
- Band SB-8 and the fact that the band was assigned by the standard on the third-night condition.
- Whether the failure falls inside a statutory filing window or the QW-4 quiet window (§6 and §7) — recorded as a determination made, or as a determination still outstanding, never left blank.

---

## 3. Who has to be told at opening

Band SB-8 notifies, at the moment the record is opened:

- **The owning team** of the settlement-recon job.
- **The platform group's shift lead.**

These two are the notification set the band mandates, and they are also the first audience of the opening notice (§5). The Escalation Roster's first rung — the platform shift lead — is therefore already informed at opening; the escalation clock in §4 begins from that notification, not from a separate later page.

Additionally, and on a clock that is not the engineering organization's to schedule:

- **The compliance office**, if the failure falls inside a statutory filing window. See §6. This obligation is carried by bands touching settlement controls, which SB-8 is.

Do not add or subtract from the opening audience for convenience. Whoever receives the opening notice receives every update and the closing notice (§5); an audience chosen loosely at opening cannot be tightened later.

---

## 4. Escalation: the garnet route and its clocks

### The ladder

The garnet route is an ordered ladder of roles, climbed one rung at a time:

1. **Platform shift lead**
2. **Duty manager**
3. **Head of platform operations**

An escalation climbs one rung at a time and **never skips a rung that has acknowledged**.

### The clocks

For the settlement family of routes:

| Rung | Role | Holds for |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Platform shift lead | **23 minutes** |
| 2 | Duty manager | **34 minutes** |
| 3 | Head of platform operations | **Until answered** — there is nowhere further to climb |

The clocks live in the Acknowledgment Clock Table, not in the roster; a clock change never edits a route, so read the table, not this document, if a clock is disputed mid-incident.

### When nobody responds — rule AC-15

- A clock that runs out **without an acknowledgment advances the call to the next rung on its own.** The engineer does not decide to escalate; expiry escalates.
- The missed rung is **recorded as missed, and is not re-tried.** Do not go back and try the shift lead again after the duty manager has been raised.
- **Acknowledging stops the climb at that rung.**
- **Declining passes the call upward immediately**, without waiting out the remainder of the clock.

Worked through, with nobody answering: the shift lead is notified at opening and holds 23 minutes. At 23 minutes with no acknowledgment, the call advances to the duty manager and that rung is marked missed. The duty manager holds 34 minutes. At 57 minutes from opening with still no acknowledgment, the call advances to the head of platform operations, and the duty manager rung is marked missed. The final rung holds until answered — the call does not lapse, expire, or return to the engineer.

### If the roster changes mid-incident

Routes change only by written agreement between the owning teams and the platform group. **An escalation in flight finishes on the roster it started on** — if the roster is edited tonight, this incident continues to climb the ladder as it stood when the record was opened.

---

## 5. What is communicated while the incident is open

Communications follow **cadence UC-11**, which applies to control-failure incidents.

### The opening notice

It must name:

- **The affected control** — the nightly settlement-recon job.
- **The days in question** — the three unagreed settlement days.
- **When the next update will arrive.**

That stated time is a **promise, not an estimate. Missing an update is itself reportable.** Choose a next-update time the shift can actually meet, including across handover.

### Every update thereafter

Each update either **reports progress** or **re-promises the next time honestly**. "Nothing to report" is an acceptable update; silence is not. A re-promise resets the promise — it does not excuse the one that was missed.

### The audience rule

Updates go to **the same audience as the opening notice**. **Narrowing the audience mid-incident is not permitted, however quiet the update.** If the incident goes quiet for two days, the two-day-later update still goes to the full opening audience.

### The closing notice

Part of the standard, not an afterthought. It goes to **the full audience** and **names the evidence the closure rests on** — that is, the CE-2 record described in §8.

### While all this is happening

**The job keeps running on its schedule.** Nothing in the incident suspends the nightly run, and the nightly run is in fact the only thing that can produce the evidence needed to close (§8).

---

## 6. The regulatory obligation, if a filing window is open

Bands touching settlement controls carry one obligation that engineering does not schedule and cannot self-serve. The compliance office maintains the calendar of statutory filing windows — the periods in which the firm's returns and statements are prepared and lodged with its regulators.

**Determine, at opening, whether the three failed nights fall inside a statutory filing window.** Windows are published a year ahead; each names its filing, its lodgment date, and the list of in-scope arrangements the filing draws on. The office confirms scope questions **in writing within a working day** — so ask in writing, early, if in-scope standing is unclear.

If a window is open and the settlement-recon control is among the in-scope arrangements:

- **Form RN-26 must be lodged with the filing before the window closes**, stating what was interrupted, the days affected, and the basis on which the filed figures stand.
- The office **can only lodge what it has been told while the window is open.**
- **Word that arrives after lodgment becomes a correction, which the regulators treat differently.** This is the one clock in this document that cannot be recovered by working harder afterwards — tell compliance early, and tell them even if you expect the job to pass tonight.

Note also: during a window, the compliance office's attention belongs to the filing rather than to new requests. Do not read a slow reply as an absence of obligation.

---

## 7. The close calendar constraint on any fix

Before making any production alteration to the settlement-recon job or to anything feeding it, check the standing of the **QW-4 quiet window** — the stretch from journal cutoff to statement sign-off, published on the finance group's internal page each period.

During QW-4, **systems whose figures flow into the statements are left as they are.** Production alterations to those systems wait until the books are signed, because an alteration mid-close turns every reconciliation difference into a question about the alteration — precisely the confusion this incident cannot afford. The controller's office grants exceptions **in writing**, and treats every exception **as a finding in the close report.**

So: if QW-4 is in force, the incident stays open and communicating (§5) while the fix waits, unless the controller's office grants a written exception. Being inside an open incident does not create the exception; only the controller's office does.

### If a re-run is the repair — procedure RP-22

Where the repair is to re-run the affected nights:

- **Re-run only after the upstream collectors have drained for the affected window.** Re-running ahead of the upstream repair reproduces the bad night. This mirrors the job's own design: a failed pass is re-attempted the following night *after the upstream statements refresh*.
- **A re-run replaces a bad night; it never appends to it.** The affected write-date partitions are replaced whole, under the feed's own prefix.
- **The original write date stays the partition's identity.** A re-run performed days later still lands under the night it repairs, so consumers re-reading the partition see the corrected records where the bad ones were. A re-run that would change a partition's write date is not a re-run — it is a new feed writing into an old feed's zone, and the layout forbids it.

---

## 8. What has to be true before the incident can be closed

**A control-failure incident closes on evidence, not on silence.** Closure requires a **CE-2 evidence record**, and CE-2 has three parts, all of which must hold:

1. **The control passes on its own schedule** — the pass comes from the scheduled run itself.
2. **Unassisted** — a manually forced pass does not qualify.
3. **The previously unagreed days are brought current** — a pass that agrees only tonight's records while the three earlier days remain unagreed is not closure.

Explicitly disqualifying, and worth stating because they are the tempting shortcuts on a long shift:

- A hand-run or forced pass, however clean its output.
- A quiet night with the control disabled — this "qualifies even less."
- Three silent nights with no failure alert and no verified pass.

**The CE-2 record is attached to the incident before the closing notice goes out**, and the closing notice names it (§5).

### Closing sequence

1. Scheduled run passes, unassisted, with the prior unagreed days brought current.
2. CE-2 evidence record assembled and **attached to the incident**.
3. Closing notice issued to the **full opening audience**, naming the CE-2 evidence.
4. Incident closed.
5. The PM-6 review record still owed — see §9. Closure does not discharge it.

---

## 9. The record the incident leaves behind

### PM-6 review record

Every closed control-failure incident files a **PM-6 review record**. It is **due on the Review Record Standard's own clock, not at closure time** — closing the incident does not close the obligation, and the review clock runs independently of how long the incident stayed open.

The record carries:

- **A timeline of the nights in question** — all three failed nights and everything after.
- **The originating conditions as they are actually understood** — not a tidy story, and not a placeholder if the cause remains genuinely unknown.
- **The corrections that will be made, each with a named owner.** A record whose corrections have no owner is **returned to the incident's owner rather than filed.** Name people, not teams.
- **The review meeting's outcome.**

Owned corrections are **tracked to completion** after filing.

### Where it lives

The record is **filed against the incident** and **referenced from the control's own operating notes** — that is, from the Settlement Recon Job Runbook — so the next operator to meet the same failure finds what the last one learned. This back-reference is part of the record, not optional tidying.

### The people side — TL-19 hours

**Hours spent on the nights in question are entered under code TL-19 before the PM-6 record is filed**, because the workforce office's ledger closes on its own rhythm whether or not the review is done.

- Ordinary working days flow in from badge records with nobody's attention. **Hours worked outside the working day are entered by hand**, with the **date and a one-line purpose**.
- Entry is due **before the payroll cutoff of the following week**.
- **An unentered line lapses.** The ledger closes with payroll and a late claim reopens nothing.
- Entered TL-19 hours accrue toward time off in lieu at the rate the employment terms set; the balance shows beside leave in the workforce portal.
- A correction to a closed period is a payroll correction: applied on the following run, adjusting pay, never the closed ledger itself. Questions about a closed period go to the workforce office in writing.

For an incident spanning three nights of out-of-hours work, this is the clock most likely to be lost — it belongs to the engineer who worked the nights, not to the incident owner.

---

## 10. On-shift checklist

**At opening**
1. Confirm three *consecutive* failed nights. Open one IN-28 record.
2. Record band SB-8. Do not adjust it.
3. Notify the owning team and the platform group's shift lead.
4. Issue the opening notice naming the control, the three unagreed days, and the time of the next update. Record the audience — it is fixed from here.
5. Start the garnet route at the shift lead. Clock: 23 minutes.
6. Determine filing-window standing; if a window is open and the control is in scope, tell the compliance office now, in writing (§6).
7. Determine QW-4 standing before proposing any production alteration (§7).

**While open**
8. Let AC-15 run the escalation: 23 min → duty manager; +34 min → head of platform operations; final rung holds until answered. Mark missed rungs missed; never re-try them.
9. Meet every promised update time, to the full audience. If you cannot make progress, re-promise honestly rather than skipping.
10. Let the job keep running on schedule.
11. If re-running, wait for upstream drain, replace partitions whole, preserve original write dates (§7).

**To close**
12. Wait for a scheduled, unassisted pass that brings the unagreed days current.
13. Assemble the CE-2 record; attach it to the incident.
14. Send the closing notice to the full audience, naming that evidence. Close.

**After close**
15. Enter TL-19 hours before the following week's payroll cutoff.
16. File the PM-6 review record on its own clock: timeline, originating conditions, corrections each with a named owner, review outcome. Reference it from the settlement-recon runbook.
17. If a filing window was open, confirm RN-26 was lodged before that window closed.

---

## Open items

These are things this document needs and the recorded material does not supply. None of them can be filled from the platform as it stands; each has to be resolved by the named party before or during execution.

1. **The identity of the owning team.** The Incident Severity Standard requires notifying "the owning team" of the settlement-recon job, but no page names it. Other pipelines' pages name owners (integrations crew, data services desk, reporting platform team, stream operations group, ingestion duty group, warehouse platform team); the settlement-recon runbook names none. Resolve before opening the record.
2. **The names behind the garnet rungs.** The roster gives roles — platform shift lead, duty manager, head of platform operations — and states explicitly that "the roster decides the names," but the recorded roster carries no names, contact channels, or current rota. Escalation cannot be executed on roles alone.
3. **The channel escalation is delivered on**, and the channel the opening/update/closing notices go out on. Neither the roster nor the communications standard names a medium.
4. **The full opening-notice audience.** SB-8 names the owning team and the platform shift lead as the ones the band notifies. Whether registered CA-9 consumers of the settlement stream also belong in the incident audience is not stated anywhere; the Consumer Agreement Ledger's notice boundary is written for *announcements* of stream change, not for incidents. Because the audience is fixed at opening and may never be narrowed, decide this deliberately with the owning team before the first notice goes out — adding consumers later is permitted, but excluding them and then wanting them in is not.
5. **The update interval under UC-11.** The standard requires the opening notice to name when the next update arrives, and treats that as a promise, but sets no default or maximum interval. The interval is the notice-writer's to choose and to honour.
6. **The PM-6 due clock.** The Review Record Standard says the record is due "on the standard's own clock rather than at closure time," but the recorded page does not state that clock's length. Ask the standard's owner; do not assume it is generous.
7. **The three failure dates.** The specific nights are not recorded in the material available here — they must be read from the job's run history and written into the record, the opening notice, and the PM-6 timeline. Today is 2026-08-10.
8. **Current filing-window standing.** Whether 2026-08-10 or the three failed nights fall inside a statutory filing window, and whether the settlement-recon control appears on that window's in-scope list, is held only in the compliance office's calendar. This is the single most time-critical unknown: after lodgment, an RN-26 becomes a correction.
9. **Current QW-4 standing.** Period dates, cutoff times, and the current window's standing are published on the finance group's internal page each period and are not available here.
10. **Where an IN-28 record is opened.** No tooling, system, tracker, or record format is named for IN-28 anywhere in the material.
11. **Who owns the incident, and who convenes the review meeting.** The Review Record Standard refers to "the incident's owner" (who receives back a record with unowned corrections) and to "the review meeting's outcome," but neither the owner-assignment rule nor the meeting's convener and attendance is recorded.
12. **The timezone the acknowledgment clocks and the nightly schedule run on**, and the job's declared LH-18 landing hour. The Delivery Expectation Standard requires every nightly feed to declare an expected landing hour, but the settlement-recon declaration is not recorded here — so "the job passed on its own schedule," the CE-2 test, has no recorded hour to be judged against.
13. **What the job actually reported on each failed night.** The runbook describes what a failed pass *means* (the day is left unagreed) but no diagnostic detail, error taxonomy, or triage step is recorded. The record must carry the failures as reported; this document deliberately does not supply a cause, because none is recorded.

# Onboarding Document — `invoice-adjustments` Nightly Feed

**Status:** pre-launch onboarding specification
**Model feed:** `parcel-events` (Parcel Events Feed Runbook)
**Prepared:** 2026-08-10

---

## 1. Purpose and scope of this document

`invoice-adjustments` is a new nightly feed to be stood up and operated exactly as `parcel-events` is operated. `parcel-events` is explicitly the feed that other nightly feeds are stood up from, and almost nothing operable lives in its own runbook: its runbook is a thin page that points at the standards it follows. Operating `invoice-adjustments` "exactly like `parcel-events`" therefore means binding it to the same six standards, in the same way:

| Concern | Governing standard | Instrument / code |
|---|---|---|
| Feed and output naming | Feed Naming Standard | pattern **FN-13** |
| Where output lands, how the area is organized | Landing Zone Layout | layout **LZ-14** |
| Storage registration and output lifetime | Storage Tier Register | tier **ST-16** |
| Expected landing time and lateness | Delivery Expectation Standard | table **LH-18** |
| Re-run after a bad night | Feed Re-run Procedure | procedure **RP-22** |
| Any copy taken off the platform | Off-platform Copy Policy | approval **EG-24** |

Two second-order registers are reached through those standards and are part of onboarding, not optional follow-up: the **Procurement Commitment Ledger** (line **PV-25**, reached through storage registration) and the **Data Sharing Agreement Register** (entry **SA-27**, reached through the off-platform copy policy).

Everything below is drawn from those recorded standards. Where the recorded material does not settle something this feed needs, that is stated in place and repeated in **Open items**.

---

## 2. Naming

### 2.1 The rule

A feed's name is its contract with everyone who schedules against it. Names follow **pattern FN-13**: **the subject first, then the grain of the records, joined with a dash**. `parcel-events` is the model the standard itself names — subject `parcel`, grain `events`.

**The output carries the feed's name.** A consumer must never need a lookup table to connect the feed to its output. This is what makes the rest of the layout self-describing: prefix, output and feed name are the same string.

### 2.2 Applied to this feed

The name `invoice-adjustments` parses under FN-13 as subject `invoice` + grain `adjustments`, joined with a dash, and is well-formed on its face. One check belongs to the owning team before launch: FN-13's second element is *the grain of the records*, so `adjustments` is correct only if the feed writes one record per adjustment. If the records are actually at some other grain (per invoice per night, per adjustment batch, per line item), the name must be settled before launch rather than after — see §2.3 for why.

The output is named `invoice-adjustments`, matching the feed. No separate or decorated output name is permitted by FN-13.

### 2.3 Renames after launch

A rename is expensive and is deliberately not a quiet operation:

- A rename runs through an **alias period**: the old name keeps working while registered consumers move over.
- The alias is retired **only when the delivery records show no reads against it** — not on a date chosen by the feed team.
- A rename performed **without** the alias period is treated as **decommissioning one feed and launching another**, with everything that obliges.

This is the reason to settle the grain before the first night rather than correcting it later.

---

## 3. Where the output lands, and how the area is organized

Governed by **layout LZ-14**.

- **One prefix per feed, named for the feed.** `invoice-adjustments` owns exactly one prefix in the landing area, named `invoice-adjustments`.
- **Everything the feed writes lands under that prefix, partitioned by write date.** There is no second area, no side location, no staging area outside the prefix.
- **Nothing writes outside its own prefix.** LZ-14 states the consequence directly: *a feed that needs a second area is two feeds*. If `invoice-adjustments` turns out to need a second output area, that is a second feed with its own name, prefix, registration and declaration — not an extension of this one.
- **Nothing but the feed writes inside the prefix.** Ownership of any object in the landing zone is readable from its path alone, and that property is the point of the layout.
- **Consumers read; they do not write.** Consumers must not write markers, checkpoints or scratch output into the `invoice-adjustments` prefix. Consumer state lives with the consumer. This applies to consumers of this feed from day one and should be stated to them at registration.

The recorded material specifies the prefix-per-feed structure and write-date partitioning, but does not record the physical location of the landing area (bucket, path root), the file format, or the literal partition-key spelling. Those are open items (§9).

---

## 4. Storage registration and how long the output lives

Governed by the **Storage Tier Register**.

### 4.1 Tier

Every feed registers its output in **exactly one storage tier**, and the tier — not the feed team — decides the output's lifetime.

Nightly operational feeds register in **tier ST-16**. `parcel-events` sits in ST-16, and the register states that a feed operated like it registers there too. **`invoice-adjustments` registers in ST-16.**

### 4.2 Lifetime

**Output in ST-16 is purged 47 days after its write date.**

Keeping anything longer is **not** a setting the feed team can change: it is a **re-registration into a retention tier**, reviewed by the register's owners. If any consumer of `invoice-adjustments` needs adjustment records beyond 47 days, that requirement must go to the register's owners as a re-registration request before it is promised to the consumer. The recorded material does not name the retention tier or its procedure.

Note the interaction with §6: purge runs from the **write date**, and a re-run preserves the original write date. A repaired partition therefore expires 47 days after the night it repairs, not 47 days after the repair.

### 4.3 Capacity — the procurement draw

Registration is also where capacity is accounted for. Platform storage is bought ahead under a standing vendor commitment, so registering `invoice-adjustments` **draws against line PV-25** of the **Procurement Commitment Ledger**, maintained by the procurement office. Registering the feed is what makes the draw visible to them.

The ledger's rules that bear on this launch:

- Draw-downs are recorded as internal registrations are made, and the office **sizes the renewal from the recorded draws** — an unrecorded draw is capacity the renewal will not cover.
- **New draws are confirmed with the vendor manager before they begin.** Standing up `invoice-adjustments` is a new draw; confirmation precedes it.
- A draw that would take PV-25 **past its committed volume waits for the renewal** rather than assuming it. If the expected volume of `invoice-adjustments` is large, the launch date is contingent on the line's headroom, not only on engineering readiness.
- Renewals run on the procurement office's own negotiation calendar. **Teams planning a large draw talk to the office a cycle ahead.**

The expected storage volume of `invoice-adjustments`, and the current headroom on PV-25, are not recorded in the available material (§9).

---

## 5. When it is expected to land, and repeated lateness

Governed by the **Delivery Expectation Standard**.

### 5.1 Declaring the landing hour

Every nightly feed **declares its expected landing hour in table LH-18**, and that declaration is what consumers schedule against. The standard is blunt about the alternative: *an undeclared feed has no lateness, only unpredictability*. Declaring `invoice-adjustments` in LH-18 is a launch prerequisite, not a post-launch tidy-up — until it is declared, the feed cannot be late, cannot be measured, and cannot be scheduled against.

**The landing hour for `invoice-adjustments` is not recorded anywhere in the available material and must be set by the owning team before launch.** The declared hour for `parcel-events` is likewise not recorded here, so it cannot simply be copied (§9).

### 5.2 What counts as late

A feed landing **after its declared hour is late**. Lateness is tracked **per morning** against the declaration.

### 5.3 What happens when it is repeatedly late

- **One late morning is noted.** No further action is prescribed.
- **Repeated late mornings in the same week are raised with the owning team as a delivery matter.** The outcome is one of exactly two things:
  1. **The window moves and the declaration is corrected** in LH-18, or
  2. **The cause is fixed.**
- **Quietly re-declaring a later hour to absorb lateness is prohibited** as a silent act: a re-declaration is a change consumers must be told about like any other. Moving the hour to make the lateness disappear without telling consumers is the specific failure the standard names.

The recorded material stops there. It does **not** tie repeated lateness to an escalation route, an acknowledgment clock, or an incident severity band; those instruments exist on this platform but the Delivery Expectation Standard does not invoke them, and neither does the `parcel-events` runbook. It also does not define "repeated" as a specific count of mornings beyond *more than one in the same week*. Both are open items (§9) — do not assume the escalation roster applies to a delivery matter.

---

## 6. Re-running after a bad night

Governed by **procedure RP-22** (Feed Re-run Procedure).

### 6.1 The core rule

**A re-run repairs a bad night by replacing it, never by appending to it.**

### 6.2 The procedure

- The **affected write-date partitions are replaced whole**, under the feed's own prefix (`invoice-adjustments`) — partial patching or appending corrected rows alongside bad ones is not a re-run.
- **The original write date stays the partition's identity.** A re-run performed days later still lands under **the night it repairs**, so consumers re-reading the partition see the corrected records exactly where the bad ones were.
- A re-run that would **change a partition's write date is not a re-run**. RP-22 classifies it as *a new feed writing into an old feed's zone*, and layout LZ-14 forbids it.

### 6.3 Ordering against upstream

Re-runs happen **after the upstream sources have drained for the affected window**. Re-running ahead of the upstream repair simply **reproduces the bad night**.

This is the point where the `parcel-events` model carries a dependency that must be reproduced, not copied. For `parcel-events`, the feed runs only after the parcel collectors drain, and a **missing hour in the output is a collector matter, not a feed matter** — re-running the feed cannot supply records a collector never delivered. The same distinction will apply to `invoice-adjustments`: some bad nights will be repairable by re-run, and some will be upstream gaps that no re-run can fill. **The upstream system that `invoice-adjustments` waits on, and the signal that tells the operator it has drained, are not recorded in the available material** and must be identified before the feed is operated (§9). Without it, the operator cannot tell the two failure classes apart, and RP-22's ordering rule cannot be followed.

### 6.4 Operator checklist for a bad night

1. Determine whether the fault is in the feed or upstream. If upstream, it is not repaired by a re-run.
2. Confirm the upstream source has drained for the affected window.
3. Identify the affected **write-date** partitions.
4. Replace those partitions **whole**, under the `invoice-adjustments` prefix, **preserving the original write dates**.
5. Do not write anything outside the prefix, and do not create a new partition for the repair date.

---

## 7. If any output is ever copied outside the platform

Governed by the **Off-platform Copy Policy**, and through it the **Data Sharing Agreement Register**.

### 7.1 It is not the operator's call

**No feed output leaves the platform on an operator's judgment alone.** This applies to `invoice-adjustments` output in every form and for every destination outside the platform.

### 7.2 The EG-24 approval

Every copy outside the platform carries an **EG-24 approval** naming three things:

1. **The receiving party**
2. **The purpose**
3. **The date the copy will be deleted**

An approval missing any of the three is **returned unactioned**. The approval is **filed before the copy is made** — not reconstructed afterwards.

**Re-copies** under an existing approval are re-copies **only while the purpose and recipient are unchanged**. A new recipient, or the same recipient for a different purpose, is a new approval.

### 7.3 The covering instrument (SA-27)

An EG-24 approval must also **cite the agreement that makes the transfer lawful**. The covering instrument is looked up in the **Data Sharing Agreement Register**, maintained by the legal office. **A transfer with no instrument to cite does not proceed, whatever its purpose.**

Register rules that bear on any `invoice-adjustments` transfer:

- Each instrument is registered as an **SA-27 entry** recording the **counterparty**, the **categories of records covered**, the **permitted purposes**, and the **instrument's expiry**.
- The citation is **checked against the entry's categories and purposes, not against the transferring team's intent**. A good-faith reading by the feed team carries no weight if invoice adjustment records are not within the entry's covered categories.
- An **expired or absent instrument means the transfer waits for the legal office**, however routine the request.
- **The register is the only authoritative list.** Copies of instruments held by teams are working copies, and **the register's expiry dates govern**.

Whether any existing SA-27 entry covers invoice adjustment records is not something the available material settles; it is resolved per transfer against the register at the time of the request.

---

## 8. What this document deliberately does not import

For completeness of instruction to whoever operates this feed: this platform also records a set of **governed-tier** obligations — change classification (**RB-7** and the change class directory), the **AN-5** consumer bulletin, the **CA-9** consumer agreement ledger, owner attestation, and finance-calendar timing constraints. Those attach to **governed-tier streams**, described as streams that feed the statutory accounts, and the model feed's own runbook does not invoke any of them.

Because `invoice-adjustments` is to be operated *exactly like* `parcel-events`, those obligations are **not** applied here. Given the subject matter, whether this feed nonetheless falls into the governed tier is a question for the owning team and the governance owners, and it is listed as an open item rather than decided in this document. If it is governed-tier, this document is a floor, not the complete set of obligations.

---

## 9. Open items

Each item below is something this document needs and the recorded material does not settle. None should be filled in by assumption.

1. **Declared landing hour.** No LH-18 declaration exists for `invoice-adjustments`, and the declared hour for `parcel-events` is not recorded in the available material, so it cannot be copied. The owning team must set and declare the hour before launch; until then the feed has no lateness, only unpredictability.
2. **Owning team and operator.** The available material does not record who owns or operates `parcel-events`, so the counterpart owner for `invoice-adjustments` cannot be derived from the model. Required, because repeated lateness is raised *with the owning team*.
3. **Upstream dependency and its drain signal.** `parcel-events` waits on the parcel collectors, and that dependency defines which bad nights are re-runnable. The equivalent upstream system for `invoice-adjustments`, and how an operator confirms it has drained for a window, are not recorded. RP-22's ordering rule cannot be followed without this.
4. **Record grain, for the FN-13 name check.** FN-13 requires the second element to be the grain of the records. Whether `invoice-adjustments` writes one record per adjustment is not recorded. Settle before launch — after launch this becomes an aliased rename.
5. **Expected storage volume and PV-25 headroom.** The volume `invoice-adjustments` will draw, and whether line PV-25 has committed volume to cover it, are not recorded. A draw beyond the committed volume waits for renewal, so this can gate the launch date.
6. **Threshold and route for repeated lateness.** The standard says repeated late mornings *in the same week* are raised with the owning team, but does not define a count, a route, an acknowledgment clock, or an incident severity band for a delivery matter. The escalation roster and incident standards exist but are not invoked by the delivery standard or by the model runbook.
7. **Physical landing-zone details.** LZ-14 fixes one prefix per feed, partitioned by write date, but the material does not record the landing area's physical root, the output file format, or the literal partition-key spelling.
8. **Retention beyond 47 days.** ST-16 purges at 47 days past write date; longer retention is a re-registration into a retention tier reviewed by the register's owners. The retention tier and its request procedure are not recorded.
9. **Governed-tier standing.** Whether `invoice-adjustments` feeds the statutory accounts, and therefore carries governed-tier obligations (change classification, AN-5 bulletins to CA-9 registered consumers, owner attestation, finance close-calendar timing), is not determined by the available material. `parcel-events` does not invoke them; the subject matter of this feed makes the question worth answering explicitly.
10. **Launch notice to consumers.** The material records a consumer-notice mechanism (AN-5 bulletins to CA-9 registered consumers) only for governed-stream *changes*. Whether standing up a new non-governed feed requires any consumer announcement or consumer registration is not recorded. Depends on item 9.
